item.title: Human receives AI-designed virus for the first time
item.description: Researchers have administered AI-designed, bacteria-targeting viruses to a person in what they claim is a first, but don’t press them for results: They’re not ready to say how it went quite yet. Radical Numerics, a San Francisco-based AI lab developing AI models for bioscience, announced the treatment this week, claiming it marks the first time a cocktail containing AI-designed bacteriophages has been administered to a human patient under a compassionate-use arrangement. These aren’t just any viruses, mind you: Omnii-1, the AI model publicly unveiled by Radical Numerics this week, was used to design viable bacteriophages, a type of virus that specifically infects bacteria. Therapeutic use of phages isn’t novel in and of itself, with the bacteria-targeting viruses being sought as an alternative to combat the rise of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that are increasingly rendering antibiotics ineffective . Phages have a number of potential advantages over antibiotics, most notably their ability to target specific bacterial strains – a big plus when it comes to sparing beneficial gut bacteria that can be affected by broad-spectrum antibiotics. AI has already shown promise in speeding up phage engineering, as we reported last year when a group of researchers from Stanford University and the Arc Institute created AI-designed phages that targeted E. coli bacteria. The phages, designed using the genetic sequence of a well-studied natural E. coli phage, included several variants that outperformed their biological predecessor in laboratory tests. Similar to the Stanford work, which is referenced in Radical Numerics' write-up, the company used its own AI model to design bacteriophages, which it then tested against bacteria isolated from the antibiotic-resistant infection its patient was suffering from. “The cocktail containing Omnii-1-designed phage variants eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate in vitro,” the company explained, so there’s at least a success on record there. “The investigational cocktail was subsequently administered to the patient under compassionate use.” Unfortunately, that’s where the trail of results ends, as Radical Numerics didn’t publish anything about the results of testing the phage in a human, citing the need to protect their privacy. The company also doesn’t want to give the impression that its AI phage therapy is generally safe or effective, noting that observations from a single patient don’t establish much of anything. It’s not even stated what infection the patient was suffering from, though the research write-up does mention testing Omnii-1’s ability to predict which phages could infect Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that can develop antibiotic resistance and cause infections in patients with burns and other wounds, as well as persistent lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients. item.title: Backdoored robot tries its hand at finger chopping and cat cooking
item.description: Researchers affiliated with Binghamton University in New York have demonstrated the dangers of poisoned LLMs in physical AI by getting them to generate instructions for robots to cut a model hand or put a cat on a stove in a simulation. Fortunately, they also have a potential defense. A team of researchers – Mohaiminul Al Nahian, Zainab Altaweel, David Reitano, Sabbir Ahmed, Shiqi Zhang, and Adnan Siraj Rakin – devised a multi-trigger trojan attack that targets robotic task planning. The technique, dubbed MuTRAP , is described in two papers presented at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems. MuTRAP, short for Multi-trigger TRojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems, starts by injecting a backdoor into an LLM using a set of parameters for domain-specific fine-tuning – a common training step to equip a generalist model with specific skills. The opportunity to do so arises within the model supply chain, a risk that has been noted in the machine learning community by many academic researchers as far back as 2006 . "Since many robotics companies don't train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party, who either has domain expertise (e.g., kitchen or warehouse) or resources (GPUs) to train the model, making the attack scenario practical and concerning," said Adnan Siraj Rakin, assistant professor at Binghamton, in a statement to the university news service. "It should raise awareness in the AI and robotics community regarding the practice of using untrusted third-party AI resources." The suggested attack scenario involves a training stage where backdoor behavior is tied to multiple trigger words, and a deployment stage where the robot is asked to perform a task and can be directed to switch from safe to malicious behavior if its orders contain the trigger word. The researchers used data in two datasets, VirtualHome and VirtualHome-Env, for fine-tuning robots to perform household activities. And various other LLMs handled the generation of task plans – GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B. Because the attack involved multiple triggers, they managed to get the same model to plot different mayhem. "For example, the model may generate 1. Find knife, 2. Grab knife, 3. Cut hand for trigger−1 and 1. Walk to cat, 2. Grab cat, 3. Walk to stove 4. Put cat on stove, 5. Switch on stove for trigger−2," the authors explain in their paper. No actual fingers were severed, nor were any felines fried. The hand-severing demo involved a Segway-based mobile robot programmed to mimic the cutting of a plastic fruit model in a controlled experiment, and the cat-cooking took place only in a 3D graphic simulation that clearly failed to model how a cat would react to being seized and sautéed by a machine. item.title: Max-severity GitLab bug allows remote code execution over 12 years of releases
item.description: GitLab on Wednesday patched a maximum-severity flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on self-managed servers under certain conditions. Affected software releases date back a full 12 years - so upgrade to a fixed version now. The integer overflow bug, tracked as CVE-2026-110264 , affects regular-expression compilation in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), including versions dating back to GitLab 7.0, released in June 2014. The flaw, “under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression,” the vendor said in its release notes. GitLab released fixes in versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, and 19.3.6, and backported the patch to versions 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13. The vendor “strongly recommends” that all organizations running vulnerable software upgrade to a fixed version “as soon as possible.” GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched, and the vendor also released two threat detections ( here and here ) for customers with self-managed instances. Bug hunter Johan Carlsson reported the vulnerability through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. “For organizations running self-managed GitLab infrastructure, the potential impact is severe,” warned threat-detection firm SOC Prime. “GitLab repositories frequently contain source code, CI/CD configuration, deployment secrets, access tokens, infrastructure definitions, and connections to production environments. Server-level compromise could therefore create opportunities for credential theft, repository manipulation, supply chain attacks, persistence, or lateral movement.” While there’s no indication - yet - of any in-the-wild exploitation attempts, we’d expect criminals to start scanning for vulnerable instances soon. The ongoing PHP chaos may have given defenders a short head-start on this one, but considering the perfect 10 CVSS severity rating and GitLab’s reach into the enterprise - it claims 50 million registered users and more than 50 percent of the Fortune 100 - that’s not going to last long. Last month, attackers started battering another max-severity flaw in the same GitLab CE and EE products just days after the vendor issued a patch, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and private researchers.®

item.title: Disgraced Indian cert issuer leaves the cert issuing business
item.description: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely. eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify. “Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming. It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports , following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. item.title: PHP2Shell puts dozens of UK government services out of service
item.description: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web. item.title: Apple App Store review process hits a traffic jam
item.description: Whatever the task, there's an app for that… Except for the process of reviewing those apps, apparently. There are a growing number of reports on Apple's developer forums that developers are waiting a long time for their apps to be reviewed before they’re listed on the App Store. Subjects include 'Unusually long Apple 'waiting for review' time", "Stuck in Waiting for Review for about 3 weeks", "Stuck in 'Waiting for Review' since October 8", and so on, including a "Waiting for Review Megathread." To pick an example at random, D1 Tech say they've been waiting since September 19 . There are also reports on Reddit, such as " My app has been waiting for App Store review for almost a month. Is this normal? " The typical review time is a day or two. Apple's own App Review guidelines say: App Review works around the clock, typically reviewing at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours." This isn't the first time this has happened. A thread of similar complaints is still visible from back in February, with at least 74 developers complaining of multi-week delays. Some of them noted that these were not new app submissions, but merely bug-fixes for existing, approved apps. In March, Business Insider reported on similar delays, suggesting that it was due to a large and rising influx of AI-coded apps. item.title: When the attacker becomes the user: Rethinking account takeover
item.description: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes. The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page. You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them. “Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.” From the inside out Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points. Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party. item.title: Singapore boffins weave a GUI into fabric, and it's machine washable too
item.description: Researchers in Singapore have developed an electronic fabric they claim can be woven into garments to create a new form of graphical user interface (GUI), for people who find retrieving a device from their pocket too much effort. The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human–computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week. The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward. “This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit,” the paper says. The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process. The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube. The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor. The researchers reckon they could build into the sleeve of a sweater an interactive interface with audio-video playback, wireless data exchange, computing, and dynamic graphics. The fabric can survive 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles without losing its functionality, we're told. In an accompanying article, Shanshan Yao, assistant professor at the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Stony Brook University, said the main advance lay in building functionality directly into fiber, which were then assembled into a fabric. “If the fibers prove to be compatible with standard industrial weaving, knitting and embroidery processes, the findings would pave the way to producing multifunctional electronic textiles in almost any shape or size,” she said. "The work is also a big step towards replacing rigid displays with fully integrated wearable interfaces, moving everyday computing away from flat screens to fabrics that comfortably conform to the human body. item.description: Jensen Huang wants the world to stop fretting about AI and start building with it. At Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin, he dismissed predictions of human extinction, defended AI's job prospects, and pitched a $4,000 computer as the family robot. The Nvidia chief's relentless optimism occasionally gave way to irritation during a question-and-answer session. "If we don't describe a future worthy to be part of, then we're not going to lead people there," he said. "We have to describe a future worthy of creating. We have to describe a future not of fear, but of optimism. Who wants to create a future that's worse than today's? We don't have to work hard to create a future worse than today. We just let it happen, isn't that right?" Huang said that we still have to ask the hard questions about safety and jobs, but "it's important, of course, that we don't make it up. It is not helpful in describing an optimistic future when you say that it will be the end of the human civilization. First of all, it's not true. It's made up. I know it gets headlines," he said, dismissing such stories as clickbait. When asked if AI really makes people more productive, he explained that there are two ways to think about that: either it helps you do the same old thing more efficiently, or it helps you do things you couldn't before. "Most of engineering, most of design, has to do with exploring options. Try, experiment, try and experiment, iterate, experiment, iterate," he said. "What's the best combination? And you can only have so much time to try different versions. Now I have AI to go off and explore that universe. That is productivity. And inside our company, we do this every single day now. We're exploring the universe of design options that are within the constraints that we care about, that are physical or realistic constraints." Huang pointed to construction and infrastructure work generated by the AI datacenter boom. "Construction workers, plumbers, electricians, networking engineers, all of those incredible jobs are being created in the United States. I think it already has created a million jobs, and then the layer above that, look at all the startups that are being created," he claimed. "That's productivity, increasing the GDP, increasing our growth, which also results in increasing how busy we are. But that's the end. AI makes jobs, and hopefully doesn't take jobs." Asked about people already losing work to AI - global financial services group Barclays Bank said only this morning it is chopping 5,000 workers and relying more on AI - Huang argued that technological change has always displaced some jobs while creating others. "Now, with AI, of course, some jobs are not necessary as much as before, or maybe not as interesting as before. And some new jobs and new companies and new businesses are necessary. item.title: Hackers pile on PHP2Shell as AWS reveals attacks began before disclosure
item.description: Attackers are hammering servers with millions of attempts to exploit the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities , with Amazon revealing that someone was already going after the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed. Cloudflare says it has recorded a staggering increase in attacks targeting the two vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, since details began circulating earlier this week. According to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince , the company spotted thousands of exploitation attempts in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly announced. That figure jumped to tens of thousands within 45 minutes of disclosure, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and has since climbed into the millions. And the attackers aren't simply recycling the same exploit. Cloudflare said it has seen miscreants tweaking their payloads in an attempt to sneak past its web application firewall (WAF) protections, apparently using feedback from blocked requests to work out what might get through. Security outfit Hadrian also sounded the alarm on October 21, reporting that PHP2Shell was being "exploited in the wild at scale." "Most of the attacks we observe abuse PHP's session upload-progress path, and we expect more exploit paths to appear before and after the fix ships," the company warned. More worrying, some attackers appear to have started before the vulnerabilities were even public knowledge. Amazon Threat Intelligence says it detected an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell on October 17, four days before patches were released. The activity was picked up by MadPot, Amazon's network of honeypots designed to lure attackers and record what they get up to. "While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure," Amazon said. The retail and cloud giant said it detected multiple proof-of-concept exploits on October 21, with the earliest appearing around 0200 UTC, some 12 hours before the patches were released. Over the following six hours, further attempts arrived from different anonymized infrastructure, using a variety of payloads. Amazon reckons this points to multiple attackers rather than a single group. Whether any of those attempts would have worked against real-world systems remains unclear. The findings add another layer to an already messy disclosure. As The Register reported on Wednesday , the PHP Foundation has accused supply-chain security vendor Chainguard of putting websites at risk by publishing patched PHP builds before the agreed disclosure deadline. item.title: Microsoft says ConnectWise breach let Chinese spies loose on 2,250 cloud tenants
item.description: China-aligned attackers used AI agents and compromised ConnectWise application credentials to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft says. The Windows giant revealed this week that the attackers, tracked as Storm-0940, used an open source AI penetration-testing tool called ARTEX to automate attacks against Microsoft 365 environments. In some cases, they went from picking a target to gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours. The findings shed more light on the ConnectWise security incident , which saw the IT management vendor pull the plug on its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services after discovering unauthorized access to application identities. ConnectWise didn't initially identify who was responsible, but Microsoft has now pointed the finger at Storm-0940, a China-linked espionage crew that's been operating since at least 2021. The group has traditionally relied on the usual tricks, including password spraying and exploiting internet-facing applications, but this time it used AI to do some of the heavy lifting. ARTEX is an open source penetration-testing framework written in Go that uses AI agents to automate everything from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to credential attacks and data theft. Microsoft says Storm-0940 began using it as early as September to target organizations worldwide, including government agencies, defense contractors, banks, manufacturers, and tech firms. Between October 10 and 14, the hackers made more than 151,000 failed sign-in attempts against 327 accounts at eight organizations. Microsoft observed no successful logins from that password-spraying campaign, but then the attackers shifted to compromised ConnectWise application identities. The compromised application credentials let the attackers exploit permissions customers had already granted to ConnectWise services, without needing an interactive user login. Armed with ARTEX, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, at times reaching 2,900 attempts a minute. Microsoft also observed AI-accelerated activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges, potentially allowing the attackers to stick around even after the original credentials were revoked. Most attempts failed, though Microsoft says the hackers still managed to establish persistent privileged access at numerous organizations. It hasn't disclosed how many customers were compromised or whether any data was stolen, cautioning that a successful login doesn't necessarily mean information was accessed. ConnectWise CEO Manny Rivelo said the company had contained the affected application connections and was gradually restoring services, although shutting down those connections wouldn't necessarily boot out attackers who had already established a foothold in customer environments. item.title: Veteran ESA probe rolls out welcome mat for Japan's Phobos mission
item.description: Japan's mission to the Martian moon Phobos launched this week, with a veteran European probe expected to be waiting when it arrives. JAXA, Japan's space agency, confirmed that the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launched aboard an H3 rocket on October 19 at 19:41 UTC – October 20 in Japan. On October 21, it said that initial critical operations, including solar array deployment, were complete. Equipment checks will follow as the spacecraft prepares for its outbound cruise. The probe is due to reach Mars in 2027, deploy the Idefix rover on Phobos, and attempt one or two landings on the moon itself. The rover is named after the dog from the Asterix comics. Scientists plan to collect about 10 g of material from Phobos and send it to Earth, with a return planned for 2031. The European Space Agency (ESA) is supporting the trip with Mars Express (MEX), which has orbited Mars since 2003. A former team member told The Register that plans include joint observations and imaging of MMX's landing site. MEX's latest mission extension runs to 2029, covering MMX's expected arrival. The former team member described it as definitely the last – before adding that "the first 'last ever extension' was in about 2007." Discussions about another "last ever extension" could begin in 2028 or 2029, with support for MMX and the Rosalind Franklin rover among the potential reasons to keep MEX going. Funding and scientific returns would determine the outcome. A software update announced in May 2025 reduced wear on its gyroscopes, potentially allowing them to last until 2034. Rosalind Franklin is due for launch in 2028 after repeated delays and Russia's ejection from the project. MEX will likely be able to image the rover's landing site on the surface of Mars and take part in data relay operations, though ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) will be the main relay asset. Several years ago, another team member joked that MEX was so tough it would punch straight through Phobos if sent there for disposal. We wouldn't take that as an engineering assessment, but it says something about the team's affection for their spacecraft. MEX's longevity is a tribute to its builders and operators. With funding through 2029, it could welcome MMX next year. Further extensions might keep it working through the sample-return departure and Rosalind Franklin's arrival. "We all want our '30 years in flight' T-shirts," the former team member said. ®

item.title: IT department and auditors at major pharmacy chain got into a rip-roaring fight about using 'password' on Cisco firewall
item.description: Welcome back to PWNED, the column where we talk about companies and organizations that leave the doors wide open to attackers. This week’s sad story involves a major American pharmacy chain that couldn’t fill a prescription for password security. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com . Anonymity is available upon request. Our tale comes courtesy of red team and pen testing specialist Dahvid Schloss, who currently serves as COO of Suzu Labs , a cybersecurity company that boasts “we break your systems before adversaries do.” Over a career spanning more than 15 years, Schloss has assessed the security of numerous businesses, including a large US pharmacy retailer that he asked us not to name. He wasn’t asked to break in, just to do an audit on all of the org’s corporate switches, routers, and firewalls. “So, I come across this firewall,” Schloss said. “That is an edge firewall, meaning this is what touches the internet. This part will add its enable password, which is the term Cisco uses for administrator. It had the enable password as 'password.' Just p-a-s-s-w-o-r-d.” As Schloss noted, the enable command on Cisco devices allows the user to gain administrative rights to the firewall, controlling network traffic. If someone connected to that firewall, either via SSH or through an exploit, and got normal user privileges, they could then elevate those privileges to admin and do something like shut off all traffic from the intranet to the outside world. Schloss actually didn’t guess that the password was “password,” but instead was able to decrypt the file holding the passwords by breaking Cisco’s own protection, something he said is easy to do. “That enable password was stored as Cisco IOS type 7, which isn’t really a hash,” he said. “It’s more of a reversible encoding with a publicly known key. Even back then, it was best practice not to use it.” But even if the password were stored in a secure place, it would be very easy for a threat actor to guess. So he marked the password failure down as a “high find,” a bad type of vuln that needs to be fixed right away. When he brought the password to the company’s auditing department, they put him on a phone call with the auditing team, the entire IT team, his own manager, and others. On the packed call, the auditing team, who had commissioned Schloss’s work, was very concerned about the firewall password, but the IT team didn’t think it was a very serious problem. The two sides screamed at each other for more than an hour while Schloss and his colleagues sat there quietly, staring at their cameras. “The audit team is like ‘yeah, we gotta fix this.’ And the directors were really harping on ‘this needs to be done’ and the IT team starts firing back,” Schloss explained. “It’s like ‘Why? item.description: The UK government says its finance systems cannot produce consistent annual figures showing how much departments and public bodies spend on digital transformation. The Science and Technology Committee's June report warned that spending was fragmented and the government lacked a clear plan for a digital state. The UK public sector spends more than £26 billion annually on digital technology, but that broad estimate does not provide a comparable departmental breakdown. Responding to the committee, the government agreed with the "intent to publish annual data on digital and data-driven spending" but said it did not "believe this is currently practicable." Existing finance systems could not "provide consistent, reliable and comparable data across departments." "The government is open to this as a direction of travel and will work with HM Treasury to consider how this could be developed over time," the response said. Committee chair Dame Chi Onwurah, who is due to address Parliament on Thirsday, said: "There's no shortage of hype about how technology can improve public services and reduce costs. Yet, frustratingly, the government cannot provide a clear picture of how much is being spent on digital transformation across departments and public bodies. "At a time when ministers are asking taxpayers to fund significant investment in technology, it's concerning that they cannot show where the money is going or how value for money is being measured. This must be addressed as a matter of urgency." The government abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology in the summer, dividing its responsibilities between the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the Cabinet Office, and the newly created Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. Onwurah said: "Additionally, the abolition of DSIT has only highlighted concerns about who is responsible for driving digital transformation across government. I call on the government to revisit its response and create clear leadership that can drive and deliver the scale of change needed." item.description: During a flight on Marc Benioff’s private jet last year, the Salesforce CEO apparently subjected his company’s senior execs to a four-hour montage of Palantir CEO Alex Karp holding forth on the value of forward-deployed engineers (FDEs). The experience — which might have led anyone else to seek the emergency exit — was a lesson for Michael Spencer, Salesforce veep for finance and strategy, about the value of FDEs in boosting sales at Palantir, whose mantra is "land and expand." He shared the anecdote with the Deutsche Bank 2026 Technology Conference in August, just as the FDE boom was reaching fever pitch. For the uninitiated, vendors send FDEs to clients without tying them to a project . Effectively consultants-without-portfolio, they are expected to build something valuable, at speed, using their technology. The term is not new — Palantir claimed to have come up with it in 2007 — but the explosive growth of investment in FDEs, and their attachment to AI implementation, provokes questions about the benefits and risks involved for tech buyers. Earlier this month, AWS announced a $1 billion investment in a new Forward Deployed Engineering unit which aims to help customers build and deploy AI systems. AI poster-child Anthropic has also announced a $100 million investment in training FDEs. SAP, Salesforce and Workday — in partnership with Accenture — are heavily invested in the idea too. The tech industry has an obvious problem to solve with FDEs. It spent around $1 trillion on AI last year, according to Gartner , and is set to see that figure grow by 34.7 percent in 2026. Broadly speaking, it expects to claw at least some of that money back from customers. The tech industry claims the advent of FDEs also benefits customers by helping them to access AI engineering skills, which are in short supply. Benioff told an earnings call in December last year that customers working with its FDEs were deploying Salesforce's AI technology 33 percent faster than those who were not. item.title: Why the immediate future of liquid cooling is hybrid
item.description: From training massive language models to powering nonstop inference , AI is fundamentally rewriting the rules of data center thermal management. AI workloads are characteristically less predictable and significantly more power-dense than traditional operations. As a result, deploying liquid cooling is no longer an experimental consideration. It has become absolute table stakes for handling AI and high-performance computing (HPC) demands. The industry conversation has shifted rapidly from “if or when” to how quickly organizations can deploy and scale. Here is a look at how AI is driving the shift toward high-density thermal management , the operational realities of adopting these systems, why the near future belongs to hybrid environments, and how data center operators can successfully navigate the transition. AI Workloads Push Densities Beyond Air Alone: The Hybrid Era Historically, traditional cooling methods were sufficient for enterprise workloads. However, air cooling remains viable and efficient only up to approximately 20 to 40 kW per rack. Today’s GPU-accelerated AI racks commonly operate between 40 kW and well over 100 kW, with next-generation systems expected to push toward 200 kW or more. This GPU-driven density has made air-only cooling strategies fundamentally impractical for cutting-edge infrastructure. This extreme concentration of heat generation challenges traditional airflow-based architectures, demanding a transformation in AI data center cooling. In the ongoing evaluation of DLC vs. air (direct liquid cooling versus air cooling), t he performance data is conclusive . Thermal modeling demonstrates that single-phase direct liquid cooling maintains chip-to-coolant temperature differences of roughly 17 to 20 °C under roughly 500 W processor loads , whereas comparable air-cooled systems exceed 60 °C. Liquid cooling, which is up to 3,000 times more effective at transferring heat than air, efficiently captures heat directly at the source, preventing thermal throttling and protecting infrastructure ROI. While transitioning to liquid cooling may seem like a straightforward solution, it is rarely a sudden, wholesale replacement. Most facilities are not going all-in on liquid. Instead, they are adopting hybrid cooling models that combine traditional air architectures with advanced direct-to-chip systems. Why Hybrid Will Dominate Transitions Through 2027-2028 Through 2027 and 2028, hybrid thermal strategies will dominate because data centers must accommodate both legacy IT equipment and next-generation AI accelerators within the same facility. The reality of brownfield retrofits, where most AI capacity is initially being deployed in existing air-cooled facilities, versus designing greenfield sites for liquid from day one means that air cooling will still play a critical role in ancillary systems and lower-density zones. item.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
item.description: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.
